Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Ravi was thirty-five, a tax consultant living in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife, Priya. No one in his office knew that before joining the firm three years ago he had spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone, delivering supplies to villages cut off by the fighting. The memory that surfaced most often—the one that still made his body lock into the same position, frozen, chest pressed against the floor, arms over his head—was the day the convoy was hit. He had been crouched behind a collapsed wall while others around him were struck. He could not recall the sequence of those minutes. The order of sounds, the order of bodies falling, none of it would stay straight. What stayed was the smoke. Dense, oily, burning everything. And the shame: he should have done something, pulled someone to cover, but he had only covered his own face.

That shame lived in him now like a second pulse. When memories came—and they came without warning, triggered by something as ordinary as a client’s raised voice in a phone call, or the faintest wisp of barbecue smoke drifting through an open window—Ravi would feel his hands fly up, palms pressed against his cheeks and forehead, as if he could hide from the memory by hiding from the room. He had stopped attending office birthday celebrations and holiday parties. Priya had noticed that he would not go to weddings or family gatherings either. When she asked why, he said he just did not feel like celebrating. What he could not tell her was that happiness felt wrong, that hoping felt like a betrayal of the people who had not survived.

At work, his concentration had frayed. He would stare at spreadsheets for minutes, the numbers blurring, his mind pulled back to that wall, that smoke, the impossible order of events. He had begun avoiding the parts of the city that reminded him of the charity’s former office, driving an extra twenty minutes to avoid a particular intersection. Every night fell heavy on him. He kept the bedroom light on until Priya turned it off; then he lay awake, listening, certain that safety was something that could be taken in an instant. Ordinary sounds made him flinch—the clatter of a dropped fork, the sudden slam of a car door outside. He knew his reactions were disproportionate, but that knowledge did nothing to stop his body from reacting.

His beliefs about the world had cracked open. He had once believed in order, in systems, in the idea that human beings could build something decent. Now he saw only chaos and failure. He felt set apart from other people, as though he carried a stain they could not see. When clients expressed even mild frustration about a tax deadline, Ravi’s stomach would knot; the anger, no matter how calm, felt like the first note of something violent.

The thing that finally brought him to seek help was the silence in his marriage. Priya had stopped asking him to go out. She had stopped asking why he covered his face when he woke from nightmares. She sat across from him at dinner and said, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” It was her sadness, not her anger, that reached him. He wanted to want to feel happy. He wanted to stop hiding from the hope that he might someday feel safe again. But when he imagined walking into a therapist’s office, the shame rose up again: he did not deserve to feel better when others had died. That was what frightened him most—that getting better might mean letting go of the guilt he had come to believe was his only remaining duty.
